text.p: Oxford Health Plans Inc founder Stephen Wiggins said Tuesday he would slacken his hourly work week but not his strategic focus on company growth after giving up the title of chief executive.

The company announced earlier Tuesday that it promoted William Sullivan to CEO, noting that he had been performing chief executive duties for the past year. But it said Wiggins, 40, would remain Oxford's chairman with more focused responsibilites.
Wiggins said giving up the CEO post was largely a quality-of-life decision.

"I've been working 60-75 hours a week and would like to get it down to 40," Wiggins said, insisting that only about 15 of those hours represented "a contribution unique to my work skills. The rest can be handled by others."

"I don't think you'll find any material change in direction of the company as a result of Bill taking over," Wiggins told Reuters late Tuesday, adding he and Sullivan had built the company together over the past decade.
"It would be a big surprise if there was any modification our our game plan," Wiggins said, noting they had similar outlooks.

He said he would continue to focus on the strategic direction of the company and lead that part of the business. "I'll continue to be responsible for a lot of new inititatives, new markets and acquisitions," Wiggins said.

In particular, he said he intended to pay special interest to bringing to maturity Oxford Specialty Management, a subsidiary launched in April 1996, which Wiggins forecast would have 1997 earnings of $100 million.
"It's a very successful start-up, and I'd like to have more time to build that business. At some point we'd like it to become an independent public company," he added.
The subsidiary pays medical specialists a fee to form their own team of doctors and other professionals to treat patients, with the hope that the collective approach will drive down medical costs.
To date, such specialty teams have treated cataracts, prostate cancer, breast cancer, coronary artery-bypass grafts and hip replacements.

Oxford's shares fell 3-11/16 to 82-1/8 on Tuesday, with some analysts attributing the slide to disappointing second-quarter health-care earnings by Aetna Inc and to concerns over the loss of Wiggins as Oxford's CEO.
"Aetna is a very unique situation," Wiggins said, adding it was still attempting to regain its equilibrium after its July 1996 merger with U.S. Healthcare.
"I understand Aetna's medical expenses are going up faster than their premiums and that they've had higher-than expected expenses," Wiggins said.
"Eventually it (the merger) will be good for them, but they have to get over the hiccups," he said, adding Oxford was not having the same problems.
Oxford's second-quarter earnings of $0.45 per share, reported Tuesday, were one cent above the First Call consensus analysts' estimate.
